message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"6.21","text":"Indeed, to take an immediate example (as I also said on another occasion), in the Caucasus Mountains the tomb of a certain Cronus, a man, is pointed out—the tomb of a savage tyrant and killer of his children. His son, named Zeus, became worse; appearing as ruler of the world by the power of magic, he breaks up many marriages, punishes his father together with his uncles, and, after he died in this way, the Cretans point out his tomb. In Mesopotamia there lie a certain Helios at Hatra and a certain Selene at Carrhae; in Egypt, a certain man named Hermes; in Thrace, Ares; in Cyprus, Aphrodite; and in Epidaurus, Asclepius. Tombs of many other such figures can also be seen.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"σῆμα","chosen":"tomb","rationale":"The word can mean a sign or monument, but the burial context and the subsequent τάφον and τάφοι support “tomb.”"},{"source_quote":"μαγείας δυνάμει κοσμοκράτωρ ἀναφανεὶς","chosen":"appearing as ruler of the world by the power of magic","rationale":"Preserves both the claimed magical means and ἀναφανείς, which presents his world-rule as an appearance or emergence rather than an unqualified fact."},{"source_quote":"σὺν τοῖς θείοις","chosen":"together with his uncles","rationale":"Nominal θείοις commonly means “uncles,” and the family context supports that sense; formally, “the divine ones” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"Ἄτροις","chosen":"Hatra","rationale":"Treated as the dative plural place-name referring to Hatra in Mesopotamia."},{"source_quote":"Ἑρμῆς ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ τις ἄνθρωπος","chosen":"in Egypt, a certain man named Hermes","rationale":"Makes explicit the apposition by which Hermes is identified as a human being without adding a claim beyond the Greek."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"καὶ οὕτως τελευτήσαντος τὸν τάφον Κρῆτες ἐπιδεικνῦσιν","issue":"The genitive absolute does not state explicitly who died. The continuing subject and the Cretan tomb tradition favor Zeus; the father is a grammatically possible but contextually less likely referent.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"6.22","text":"Thus it has been plainly acknowledged by those who think correctly that they were human beings. Those who were their contemporaries, realizing that they had proved mortal, paid less heed to them after they died; but the long passage of time placed the reputation of gods around them. Do not be amazed if those who lived in the days of Asclepius and Heracles were deceived, or in the days of Dionysus or anyone else of that period, since even Hector at Ilium and Achilles on the island of Leuce are worshiped by the people there, Patroclus by the Opuntians, and Alexander the Macedonian by the Rhodians.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἄνθρωποι γεγενῆσθαι ὡμολόγηνται","chosen":"it has been plainly acknowledged ... that they were human beings","rationale":"The implied subjects are the allegedly divine figures discussed in the preceding section; γεγενῆσθαι identifies them as having been humans."},{"source_quote":"ὑπαισθόμενοι αὐτοὺς θνητοὺς γεγονέναι","chosen":"realizing that they had proved mortal","rationale":"Ὑπαισθάνομαι can mean perceive or come to suspect, while γεγονέναι here points to their demonstrated mortal condition."},{"source_quote":"δόξαν θεῶν αὐτοῖς περιέθηκεν","chosen":"placed the reputation of gods around them","rationale":"Retains the source image of time clothing or surrounding them with divine reputation rather than merely saying that time made them gods."},{"source_quote":"οἱ κατὰ Ἀσκληπιὸν καὶ Ἡρακλέα γενόμενοι","chosen":"those who lived in the days of Asclepius and Heracles","rationale":"The surrounding argument concerns contemporaries and the effects of elapsed time. “Those associated with Asclepius and Heracles” remains a possible reading of οἱ κατά."},{"source_quote":"ὅπου καὶ","chosen":"since even","rationale":"Here ὅπου introduces the striking circumstance that supports the preceding warning, rather than denoting a literal location."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"6.23","text":"But among the Egyptians, even now, a man is worshiped as a god before his death. This, at least, is a lesser act of impiety, because the Egyptians accord divine honors while a man is alive; but the most ridiculous thing of all is that they worship birds and reptiles and all animals. For most human beings neither think nor act with judgment at all. Now observe what is most shameful of all: the one who, by their account, is father of gods and humans, whom most people call Zeus, they depict in a painting as a goose coupled with Leda and set up publicly. For retribution for this outrage, I would have liked it if they had portrayed their present king in a shameful coupling and, having done the same thing they have dared to do in Zeus’s case, had set it up publicly, so that, even if only through the anger of their temporary king—and he a human being—they might learn through punishment that due honor must be rendered. I tell you these things not as one who has already recognized the God who truly is, but, being fair-minded, I confess: Though I do not know what God is, still I think I know clearly that God exists.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"θείας τιμὰς νομίζουσιν","chosen":"accord divine honors","rationale":"Νομίζω can denote customary observance or acknowledgment; in this context it concerns treating a living person as entitled to divine honors."},{"source_quote":"τὸν δι’ αὐτῶν ὄντα πατέρα θεῶν τε καὶ ἀνθρώπων","chosen":"the one who, by their account, is father of gods and humans","rationale":"The phrase δι’ αὐτῶν is literally “through them.” “By their account” expresses that his status is established by their own representation or claim; “through their agency” is a more literal alternative."},{"source_quote":"Λήδᾳ συνεσχηματισμένον χῆνα","chosen":"as a goose coupled with Leda","rationale":"Χῆνα explicitly means “goose,” not the familiar “swan.” The participle describes Zeus as joined or correspondingly formed with Leda and, in this sexual context, is rendered “coupled with.”"},{"source_quote":"ἐπὶ αἰσχρᾶς πλοκῆς","chosen":"in a shameful coupling","rationale":"Πλοκή can mean an entwining or entanglement; the preceding image of Zeus and Leda supports the sexual sense “coupling.”"},{"source_quote":"τοῦ προσκαίρου βασιλέως","chosen":"their temporary king","rationale":"Πρόσκαιρος emphasizes that the ruler is only for a limited time, sharpening the contrast with the honor owed to deity."},{"source_quote":"Εἰ καὶ τί θεὸς οὐκ οἶδα, ἀλλ’ οὖν γε σαφῶς ὅτι θεός, νομίζω εἰδέναι","chosen":"Though I do not know what God is, still I think I know clearly that God exists","rationale":"The contrast is between knowing what God is and knowing that God is. “That he is God” is grammatically possible, but it supplies a less evident personal referent."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἤθελον εἰ τὸν τοῦ καιροῦ βασιλέα αὐτῶν γράψαντες ἐπὶ αἰσχρᾶς πλοκῆς, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τοῦ Διὸς τετολμήκασιν ποιῆσαι, οὕτω ποιήσαντες ἀνέθεσαν δημοσίᾳ","issue":"The printed construction with ἤθελον εἰ followed by aorist indicatives is compressed. It defensibly expresses an unreal wish, “I would have liked it if they had ...”; an alternative is “I wanted to see whether they had ...,” though that fits the argument less well. No correction is required for the selected rendering.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"6.24","text":"To take an immediate example, the first four elements—things brought into being by another—cannot be God; neither can mixing, blending, coming-to-be, the visible vessel that encompasses the whole, the sediment collecting in Hades, the water floating on top, the boiling substance, or the air extending from it as far as the things here. For whether the four elements had stood apart from one another—in which case they could not have been mixed for the generation of a living creature without some great craftsman—or had always been joined to one another, even so they are fitted together by a craftsman mind to suit what belongs properly to the limbs and parts of the living creature, so that it can preserve the proportion of each part to every other, possess a well-bounded constitution, and have all its inward parts receive the appropriate harmony. Likewise, the craftsman mind precisely determines the proper places of each with complete beauty. To sum up: as for all the other things, everything a living creature must have, the craftsman mind left nothing lacking in this great living creature of the entire revolving sphere.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὰ ὑπὸ ἄλλου γενόμενα","chosen":"things brought into being by another","rationale":"The phrase modifies the four elements and supplies the reason they cannot themselves be God."},{"source_quote":"τὸ πᾶν περιέχον ὁρατὸν κύτος","chosen":"the visible vessel that encompasses the whole","rationale":"Κύτος denotes a hollow body, cavity, or vessel. “Vessel” preserves the cosmological container image without identifying it more specifically than the Greek does."},{"source_quote":"ἡ ἐν τῷ ᾄδῃ συρρέουσα ὑποστάθμη","chosen":"the sediment collecting in Hades","rationale":"Ὑποστάθμη denotes sediment, dregs, or what settles at the bottom, while συρρέουσα presents it as flowing or gathering together."},{"source_quote":"ὁ ἐξ αὐτῆς μέχρι τῶν ἐνταῦθα διήκων ἀήρ","chosen":"the air extending from it as far as the things here","rationale":"The feminine pronoun most naturally refers to the immediately preceding “boiling substance.” “The things here” preserves the indefinite τῶν ἐνταῦθα."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τὸ οἰκεῖον τῶν τοῦ ζῴου μελῶν καὶ μερῶν συναρμόζεται","chosen":"are fitted together by a craftsman mind to suit what belongs properly to the limbs and parts of the living creature","rationale":"The phrase describes an intelligent fitting of the elements to the proper constitution or function of the creature’s members and parts."},{"source_quote":"τὴν ἕξιν εὐπερίγραφον ἔχῃ","chosen":"possess a well-bounded constitution","rationale":"Ἕξις here is the creature’s condition or constitution, and εὐπερίγραφος suggests something readily circumscribed or clearly bounded; “well-defined constitution” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"τῷ μεγάλῳ τούτῳ ζῴῳ τῆς ὅλης περιφορᾶς","chosen":"this great living creature of the entire revolving sphere","rationale":"The cosmos is presented as a great living creature. Περιφορά denotes revolution, circular motion, or the circuit produced by it; “the whole cosmic circuit” is an alternative."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἵνα τὴν ἑκάστου πρὸς ἕκαστον ἀναλογίαν ἀποσώζειν δύνηται καὶ τὴν ἕξιν εὐπερίγραφον ἔχῃ","issue":"The singular verbs leave their subject implicit. The living creature or resulting organized whole is the best contextual referent; taking the craftsman mind as subject is less natural but grammatically conceivable.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"6.25","text":"Thus there must be some unoriginated craftsman mind that either gathered the elements when they were apart or, when they were together with one another, skillfully blended them for the generation of a living creature and completed a single work from them all; for it is impossible for an exceedingly wise work to be completed without some greater mind. Nor indeed can love be the craftsman of all, nor desire, nor force, nor anything else of that kind, since such things are passions and by nature come and go. Nor is anything moved by another God, or anything altered by time or nature and dissolved into no longer existing.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"νοῦν ἀγέννητον τεχνίτην","chosen":"unoriginated craftsman mind","rationale":"Ἀγέννητος means not generated or not brought into being. “Unoriginated” fits the contrast with elements produced by another; “unbegotten” is a possible but more traditionally theological rendering."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς ζῴου γένεσιν τεχνικῶς ἐκέρασεν","chosen":"skillfully blended them for the generation of a living creature","rationale":"Τεχνικῶς emphasizes artful or craftsmanlike arrangement, and πρὸς with γένεσιν expresses its purpose."},{"source_quote":"πάνυ σοφὸν ἔργον","chosen":"an exceedingly wise work","rationale":"The adjective presents the work as embodying extraordinary wisdom or skill; “a work of surpassing skill” would express the same implication more idiomatically."},{"source_quote":"ἔρως","chosen":"love","rationale":"The noun can denote love as a cosmic principle and may be personified as Eros. Lowercase “love” avoids imposing personification while retaining the proposed causal principle."},{"source_quote":"συμβαίνειν καὶ ἀποβαίνειν πέφυκεν","chosen":"by nature come and go","rationale":"The paired verbs describe passions as contingent occurrences that arise and depart, in contrast to an unoriginated craftsman."},{"source_quote":"τὸ ὑφ’ ἑτέρου φερόμενον","chosen":"anything moved by another","rationale":"Φέρω in the passive can mean being borne, carried, or moved. “Moved” best expresses the causal contrast, while “carried along by another” is a more concrete alternative."},{"source_quote":"εἰς τὸ μηκέτι εἶναι ἀναλυόμενον","chosen":"dissolved into no longer existing","rationale":"Preserves the source’s image of dissolution terminating in nonexistence rather than reducing it to the single word “destroyed.”"}],"source_issues":[]}]}
